items.title: Another Day of Protests Unfurls in France’s Autumn of Discontent
items.summary: Two days after a general strike and huge demonstrations, students and workers took to the streets again on Saturday.
items.full_text:
Title: Another Day of Protests Unfurls in France’s Autumn of Discontent - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/europe/france-fourth-saturday-protests.html

Published Time: Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:33:04 GMT

Markdown Content:
French students and workers rallied for a fourth consecutive Saturday in Paris and other cities, two days after a [general strike](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/world/europe/france-protests-general-strike.html?searchResultPosition=1) brought more than half a million people into the streets.

The students are [protesting the disrepair of their schools](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/france-school-protest-paul-eluard.html) and an unpopular university admissions process; workers are demanding higher wages and improved public services. The crowds have remained large since the protests [evolved last month](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/06/world/france-protests-students-schools) from a student-focused movement to a national one, suggesting the depth and breadth of grievances in the country.

“I came to support the youth; I find their claims to be legitimate,” said France Lucat, 44, who traveled 25 miles to join the demonstration in Paris. “And I am also very shocked by the police violence.”

It was the first time she joined since the recent protests began, she said. She had feared it could be unsafe, having seen coverage of the unrest, but chose to come and see for herself. Next week, she would bring her children, she said. “That’s also why I came,” she said, “because I am afraid, and I shouldn’t be afraid.”

Her sister, Alice Courtieux, 52, held a sign saying “Macron You Trumped Us!” to protest what she called “the drift toward the right and the far right by this authoritarian government.” Both women expressed frustration with the lack of response to the demands of students and workers. But, Ms. Courtieux said, “It’s by joining demonstrations that you find hope again.”

Image

Police officers and protesters in Paris on Saturday.Credit...Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

In an early assessment, the interior ministry said there had been a “clear decline” in the number of protesters across the country compared with previous Saturdays. “The situation across the entire territory remains generally calm and under control,” the ministry added, noting that 18 people had been arrested so far and that the authorities had carried out more than 15,000 spot checks to prevent people from taking weapons to protest areas. Some 70,000 police officers were on the streets on Saturday, matching the deployment for the last three major protests.

This week, the prime minister’s office announced that it would hold a “social conference” on Monday with organizations representing business leaders and workers to discuss wages and the cost of living. Separate meetings with civil servants unions and with representatives of high school students are also planned for next week. Additionally, there will be a meeting with students, parents, teachers and lawmakers dedicated to the overhaul of the college admission platform, which students have harshly criticized.

“It is time for the government to finally acknowledge that there is a real issue regarding purchasing power,” Marylise Léon, the head of the C.F.D.T., one of the country’s main workers’ unions, said on Friday in a broadcast interview. “So, we need to sit down at the table, keeping in mind that it is also, ultimately, the responsibility of employers to provide decent wages.”

On Thursday, the marches were mainly peaceful, though protesters clashed with the police in Lyon, where a car was set on fire.

The government has tried to avoid a repeat of [Oct. 17](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/17/world/europe/france-protest-riots-marseille.html), when protests degenerated into [arson](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/world/france-limoges-fire-arson-protests.html), [looting](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/31/world/europe/france-riots-protests-paris-rue-beaurepaire.html) and other violence. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said fewer groups had applied for permission to hold rallies than on Thursday, but there was still the potential for spontaneous protests and the clashes that often follow.

While there have been no fatalities caused by the violence — one person died of cardiac arrest during the Oct. 17 rally — the strain on France’s police and security services appeared to be spilling into other areas.

Image

A demonstration in Bordeaux, France, on Saturday.Credit...Philippe Lopez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

The foreign ministry announced on Thursday that it would move a high-level diplomatic meeting to Paris from Marseille next week, citing “logistical and operational” reasons. The meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 7 advanced industrial nations had been planned for Nov. 9 and 10 in the Pharo Palace, a 19th-century building, less than a mile from streets looted on Oct. 17, that overlooks Marseille’s harbor.

But the government opted to move the meeting at the last minute because, officials said, it fell just before the Paris Peace Forum, a conference that gathers world leaders to discuss war, peace and conflict resolution.

[Marseille](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/24/world/europe/france-looting-rue-paradis-marseille.html) and Paris have both been hit by violence, which tends to erupt as the police disperse protesters at the end of marches. The authorities have also been dealing with a [number of fake bomb threats](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/world/europe/bomb-threats-planes-flights-europe-travel.html) against commercial flights in Europe, several of which were crossing French territory.

“It was a combination of logistical and operational considerations that led us to decide, as the deadline approached, to relocate the event to Paris,” Pascal Confavreux, a spokesman for the ministry, said on Thursday.

Mr. Confavreux did not address the protests or bomb threats specifically. But he said there were “operational issues for the teams, involving protocols and logistics, with two extremely important events taking place back-to-back. And that’s why it was important that we not overburden the teams.”

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

items.title: How Cardiologists’ High Hopes for Two Drugs Were Dashed
items.summary: By every measure, the drugs were no better than placebos, full data revealed on Saturday. Was it the fault of the design of the studies, or our very hypotheses about heart disease?
items.full_text:
Title: How Cardiologists’ High Hopes for Two Drugs Were Dashed - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/07/science/heart-drugs-failed-novartis-novo-nordisk.html

Published Time: Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:26:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
Cardiologists have been on edge for months, waiting for the details surrounding recent reports of [the stunning failures](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/11/science/heart-drug-failed-novartis.html) of two new heart drugs.

The drugs — pelacarsen and ziltivekimab — were widely expected to usher in a new era in preventing heart disease. Companies, betting on the drugs’ promise, made huge investments in developing them.

So when doctors [saw preliminary announcements](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/science/heart-drug-fails-novartis-pelacarsen.html) that the drugs [were not helping patients](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/06/science/heart-disease-drug-fails-novo-nordisk.html) in large clinical trials, many felt blindsided, although still hopeful that there was more to the story than they knew.

“The whole cardiovascular community was gobsmacked,” said Dr. Karol Watson, a director of UCLA’s preventive cardiology program.

Were the drugs close to succeeding, just barely missing a statistically significant benefit? Or were there at least subgroups of patients who were helped?

Now the answers are in. There was not a shred of evidence that the drugs helped anyone. By every measure, they were no better than placebos.

The results, Dr. Watson noted, “are about as neutral as they can be.” The full data were presented on Saturday morning at the annual meeting of the American Heart Association and in simultaneous publications in The New England Journal of Medicine.

One drug, pelacarsen, by Novartis, is known to make levels of the Lp(a) blood protein plunge. The protein is widely believed to cause heart attacks and strokes. The other, ziltivekimab, by Novo Nordisk, stops inflammation, thought to be a major component of plaques in arteries. Neither drug made a dent in heart disease outcomes during these clinical trials.

Dr. Paul Ridker of Mass General Brigham, who was the principal investigator for the inflammation trial — known as the Zeus study — had been a true believer.

He was convinced by suggestive evidence that squelching inflammation could protect people from heart disease. There was, he said, an earlier encouraging study involving an experimental [anti-inflammatory drug](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1707914) made by Novartis, as well as studies indicating that colchicine, an anti-inflammatory drug used to treat gout, could also be protective.

Until the day he saw the results, Dr. Ridker said in a recent interview, he had thought the Zeus study was “a brilliant idea,” bound to show that the Novo drug, ziltivekimab, which blocks an inflammatory protein called il-6, was effective. The participants all had severe heart disease, advanced kidney disease and a blood protein that is a marker of inflammation.

Instead of protecting patients in Zeus, though, Dr. Ridker announced on Saturday that [no one had been helped](http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2612126) by the drug. Every subgroup of patients in the 6,376-patient study fared the same. Those taking the drug did no better than those taking a placebo, even though the drug did reduce inflammation.

“Did we pick the wrong target, the wrong patient population?” Dr. Ridker said.

Or did the patients have heart disease that was so advanced it could not be helped? “Maybe the horse was out of the barn,” he said.

Others in the field are wondering if the hypothesis itself was wrong. Maybe inflammation is a sign of disease, not a cause, as white hair is a sign of aging.

Novo announced in September that it was stopping two other studies of ziltivekimab that involved patients with heart failure. An independent committee determined that the drug was not helping them. The company is continuing to test its drug in patients who have had a heart attack. That study will conclude next year.

Dr. Ridker, who proposed the link between inflammation and heart disease more than a quarter-century ago, has not given up hope. He noted that there was genetic and epidemiological evidence as well as evidence from animal studies that a different protein in the same inflammation pathway should protect against heart attacks and strokes.

“We already know this is going to work,” Dr. Ridker said. Now, he added, the question is: “How do we find the right drug for the right patient?”

The principal investigator for Horizon, the Lp(a) study, is Dr. Steven Nissen of the Cleveland Clinic. He said his concern was that the study’s [disappointing results](http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2610159) would lead patients to drop out of two other studies testing drugs that reduce Lp(a) levels.

“A single trial doesn’t necessarily give us all the answers,” Dr. Nissen said. And, he added, high levels of Lp(a) are “a powerful risk factor.” It remains possible, he said, that patients in the Horizon trial had heart disease so advanced that it was too late for the Novartis drug to help.

Another hypothesis was that the patients’ other risk factors — blood pressure and L.D.L. cholesterol — were so well controlled that their risk was about as low as it could go, said Dr. Roger Blumenthal, director of the Johns Hopkins Ciccarone Center for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease. Reducing Lp(a) levels could not lower it further.

Dr. Ridker had another idea. All the Horizon patients were taking anti-clotting medications. Lp(a) is thought to cause heart disease by promoting blood clots. Perhaps the anti-clotting medications diluted the drug’s effects.

But the bottom line was that, for whatever reasons, the Novartis drug had utterly failed.

“Was there anything that we could point a finger to that said, ‘Yeah, there’s a benefit’?” Dr. Nissen asked.

No, he added, “there was nothing.”

items.title: Here’s the latest.
items.full_text: Hiring was unexpectedly strong in October, when employers added workers at a vigorous pace. Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, and the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1 percent. Job gains for August and September were revised upward by a total of 84,000 positions. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent compared with the same time last year. The report reaffirmed the general picture of the labor market as healthy. Employers have broadly continued to hire despite President Trump’s volatile tariff policy, the war in Iran that has cranked up energy price and uncertainty over artificial intelligence. Businesses have held onto their workers, keeping layoffs at historically low levels. And employees have been reluctant to leave their jobs. Here’s what to know: Short-term strength, long-term stability: Employers have been adding workers at a slow but steady pace for months. The unemployment rate has stayed low, hovering in a narrow range for the last two years. The robust October report underscored the labor market’s resilience but did not change this overall picture. Trouble spots: Though the labor market has remained solid, people who are looking for work, including recent college graduates, have found limited opportunities. And even those who do have jobs have been losing leverage, as wage growth has slowed and inflation has continued to erode their spending power. Those factors could help explain why so many Americans are feeling dour about the economy. A.I. jitters : One big question hanging over the labor market is the impact of artificial intelligence. So far, the technology does not appear to be leading to widespread job losses. But there are some indications that the rise of the technology is depressing hiring, particularly for entry-level positions in sectors including financial services and information. Green shoots? There have been some tentative signs that the labor market may be on the verge of perking up. The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey this week showed that the quits rate rose in September, a sign that workers may be feeling more confident in their ability to get new jobs. Show more Nov. 6, 2026, 11:02 a.m. ET Job seekers wait in line at a job fair in New York in October. Credit... Seth Wenig/Associated Press Is artificial intelligence taking our jobs? It’s arguably the single biggest question facing the labor market right now, all the more so after Tuesday’s midterm elections showed widespread public animosity toward A.I. and data centers, in particular. The evidence, though, is far from clear. White-collar industries like accounting, legal services and finance mostly added jobs in October, but their growth has been decidedly weak over the past few years. The information sector — a broad category that includes much of tech but also media companies — has been cutting jobs steadily since late 2022. Microsoft last week announced that it was offering buyouts to tens of thousands of employees , making it the latest tech giant to cut jobs. Economists are cautious about attributing that softness to A.I., however. Other forces, such as high interest rates and shifting demand patterns following the pandemic, could also be playing a role. And despite announcements like Microsoft’s, layoffs remain low, even in white-collar sectors. Similarly, some economists have highlighted relatively high rates of unemployment among younger workers, especially young college graduates, as evidence that A.I. is displacing entry-level jobs. But that, too, could be the result of other factors, including the generally low rate of hiring and turnover, which is particularly hard on people trying to break into the job market. To the extent there is a consensus among economists, it looks something like this: A.I. hasn’t had a striking effect on employment, but it may be starting to show up in some corners of the labor market. Even if A.I. is taking a toll on hiring, it isn’t quite clear what that means. Are companies using A.I. to replace workers? Or merely pressing “pause” on hiring while they figure out where these new tools will be most useful? Or are they spending so much on tokens and A.I. infrastructure that they are looking to cut costs elsewhere? Those explanations could all look similar in the moment, but have very different implications over the longer run. The impact of A.I. is showing up clearly in one place, however: blue-collar jobs. The data center build out is helping to prop up employment in the construction sector, even as high interest rates have led to a sharp pullback in home building. Demand for chips and other A.I. equipment is also creating jobs in manufacturing, offsetting losses elsewhere in the sector. The future of that boom now looks uncertain following this week’s election results, however. The plunge in share prices for tech companies on Thursday — partly reversed on Friday — reflected investors’ concern that public backlash to data centers could lead to a slowdown in construction, which could have broader economic implications given the extent to which A.I. has been driving growth.
